tips.title: Count the carbon in the COOH
tips.body: CH₃COOH has **two** carbons — one in the CH₃, one in the COOH — so it is **ethan**oic acid. And methanoic acid is HCOOH because its only carbon is inside the functional group, leaving nothing to write in front.

tips.title: Alcohol first, acid second
tips.body: An ester's name is built in two halves: ethanol gives **ethyl**, ethanoic acid gives **ethanoate**, so the ester is **ethyl ethanoate**. Write the two halves down separately and the order stops being something you have to recall.

tips.title: Weak is not dilute
tips.body: **Weak** means **partially ionised** and belongs to the acid itself; **dilute** means little acid per unit volume and belongs to the solution. A concentrated weak acid exists, and adding water never turns a strong acid into a weak one.

tips.title: One pH unit is ten times
tips.body: pH 2 against pH 5 is three units, so $10 \times 10 \times 10 = 1000$ times the hydrogen ions. Count the units and raise 10 to that power — no calculation harder than that is ever asked.

tips.title: No equations needed here
tips.body: You are not expected to balance any equation for a reaction of a carboxylic acid. Describe what happens and name the products. The marks that are actually hard to get are on the **ionisation** explanation.

why.matters:
Swap the –OH of an alcohol for a **–COOH** and the molecule becomes an acid: it releases H⁺ in water, turns litmus red, fizzes with a carbonate. One group is the difference between something neutral and something sharp enough to taste.

Then react an acid with an alcohol and the two groups join into an **ester**, which is neither: it does not dissolve much, it does not react with much, and it smells. Three families, one functional group apart.

examples.title: The sharp taste is a functional group
examples.body:
Vinegar, a lemon, sour milk and an aching muscle after a sprint all contain a carboxylic acid — ethanoic, citric, lactic. They taste and behave alike because they carry the same **–COOH**, whatever else is attached.

That is what a functional group buys you. You do not have to learn each acid separately: they all release H⁺ in water, all turn litmus red, and all fizz with a carbonate to give carbon dioxide — which is exactly why vinegar clears limescale and lemon juice cleans a copper pan.

visual.alt: A table of four carboxylic acids and where each is met: ethanoic acid in vinegar, citric acid in lemons and sherbet, lactic acid in sour milk and tired muscles, and methanoic acid in an ant sting

examples.title: The smallest acid there is, and the ant that uses it
examples.body:
Methanoic acid is a carboxylic acid with a single carbon — the whole molecule is the functional group with one hydrogen attached. It is what an ant sprays when it bites, and its old name, formic acid, comes from the Latin for ant.

Being the smallest makes it the easiest to draw, and the drawing shows what a carboxylic acid actually is: a carbon with a **double bond to one oxygen** and a **single bond to an O–H**. That second oxygen is what makes the hydrogen easy to lose, and the molecule an acid.

examples.title: Why a sweet smells of pear drops
examples.body:
Esters are made by joining a carboxylic acid to an alcohol, with an acid catalyst, and the water that is left over is squeezed out between them.

What comes out is a family of molecules whose main property is their **smell**. Ethyl ethanoate is the solvent in nail polish remover; its relatives are the pear drop, the banana and the pineapple in a sweet shop, and much of what is on the label as *flavouring*. Two dull-smelling liquids, joined, give one that is anything but.

steps.title: The -COOH group
steps.body:
A **carboxylic acid** contains the functional group **–COOH**, a carboxyl group. That is one carbon carrying **two** oxygens: one joined by a double bond, and one in an **O–H**.

The first four members are **methanoic, ethanoic, propanoic and butanoic acid**. These four names are the only ones you need.

They are written as:

- HCOOH — methanoic acid
- CH₃COOH — ethanoic acid, the acid in vinegar
- C₂H₅COOH — propanoic acid
- C₃H₇COOH — butanoic acid

Count the carbons carefully. In CH₃**COOH** there are **two** carbons — one in the CH₃ and one in the COOH — so it is **ethan**oic acid, with two carbons like ethane and ethanol. The carbon of the functional group counts towards the name.

That is also why methanoic acid is **H**COOH: its single carbon is the one in the COOH, so there is nothing left to put in front but a hydrogen.

steps.title: Three things carboxylic acids do
steps.body:
The spec names three reactions, and you should be able to describe each.

**1. With carbonates.** They **fizz**, giving off **carbon dioxide**, and leave a salt and water. This is the ordinary acid–carbonate reaction, and it is the test that shows a carboxylic acid is genuinely acidic.

**2. Dissolving in water.** They dissolve, and the solution is **acidic** — pH below 7. But only **partially ionised**, so the pH is **higher** than a strong acid of the same concentration. More on that below.

**3. With alcohols.** In the presence of an **acid catalyst**, a carboxylic acid and an alcohol react to form an **ester**. Ethanoic acid and ethanol give **ethyl ethanoate** — the only ester whose name you need.

You are **not** expected to write balanced equations for any reaction of a carboxylic acid. What is marked is describing what happens and naming the products correctly.

A carboxylic acid plus an alcohol makes an **ester**, with an **acid catalyst**. Esters have strong, sweet, fruity smells, and are used in perfumes and food flavourings.

steps.title: Strong and weak: a Higher tier idea
steps.body:
This section is **Higher tier only**. It explains why carboxylic acids are **weak** acids.

When an acid dissolves in water it **ionises** — it releases **hydrogen ions, H⁺**, and those ions are what make a solution acidic.

- A **strong** acid is **completely** ionised: essentially every molecule releases its H⁺. Hydrochloric, nitric and sulfuric acids are strong.
- A **weak** acid is only **partially** ionised: at any moment most of the molecules have not released their H⁺. Ethanoic, citric and carbonic acids are weak.

Carboxylic acids are **weak acids**, so for the **same concentration** a carboxylic acid gives **fewer hydrogen ions** than a strong acid, and therefore a **higher pH**.

The numbers are worth knowing precisely. As pH **decreases by one unit**, the hydrogen ion concentration goes **up by a factor of 10**. So a solution at pH 1 has **100 times** the hydrogen ion concentration of one at pH 3.

**Weak is not the same as dilute**, and this is the distinction the question is really testing:

- **Strong or weak** is about the **degree of ionisation** — a property of the acid itself.
- **Dilute or concentrated** is about **how much acid there is** in a given volume of solution.

So a concentrated solution of a weak acid is perfectly possible, and so is a dilute solution of a strong one.

steps.title: Going deeper: weak against dilute, and counting carbons
steps.body:
**The distinction that carries the marks.** *Weak* and *dilute* are not synonyms, and a question that uses both words is testing exactly that:

- **Weak** — the acid is only **partially ionised**. A property of the **substance**, and it cannot be changed by adding water.
- **Dilute** — there is **not much acid** in a given volume. A property of the **solution**, and it changes the moment you add water.

So *concentrated ethanoic acid* is a perfectly sensible phrase: a lot of a weak acid. And *dilute hydrochloric acid* is a little of a strong one. An answer that says ethanoic acid is weak *because it is dilute* has the idea backwards.

**What weak does and does not change.** A weak acid still reacts with carbonates, still neutralises alkalis, and still forms the same salts — because the reactions are the same. What changes is the **rate** and the **pH**: fewer hydrogen ions at any moment means a **higher pH** and a **slower** reaction at the same concentration.

**Counting carbons.** The carbon in the –COOH counts towards the name, which trips people up in both directions:

- CH₃COOH has **two** carbons, so it is **ethan**oic acid, not methanoic.
- Methanoic acid is **H**COOH, with its only carbon inside the functional group.

The same rule holds when an alcohol is oxidised: ethanol (2 carbons) gives ethanoic acid (2 carbons). The chain does not get longer.

**Esters, named in two halves.** The **alcohol** gives the first word and the **acid** gives the second: ethanol + ethanoic acid → **ethyl ethanoate**. Write the halves down separately before joining them, and the order stops being something to remember.

**What you are not asked to do.** No balanced equations for any reaction of a carboxylic acid, and no ester names beyond ethyl ethanoate. Effort spent there is effort not spent on the ionisation explanation, which is where the Higher tier marks actually are.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- A **carboxylic acid** has the functional group **–COOH**: one carbon with a double-bonded O and an O–H.
- The first four are **methanoic, ethanoic, propanoic and butanoic acid**.
- The carbon in the –COOH **counts** towards the name, so CH₃COOH is **ethan**oic acid, with two carbons.
- **With carbonates**: fizzing, giving **carbon dioxide**, plus a salt and water.
- **In water**: dissolve to give an **acidic** solution, pH below 7.
- **With alcohols**: an **acid catalyst** gives an **ester** and water.
- Ethanoic acid + ethanol → **ethyl ethanoate**, the only ester you need to name.
- The **alcohol** names the first half of an ester, the **acid** the second.
- Carboxylic acids come from **oxidising alcohols** — ethanol gives ethanoic acid.
- **Higher tier**: carboxylic acids are **weak acids**, only **partially ionised**, so at the same concentration they give **fewer hydrogen ions** and a **higher pH**.
- Each pH unit down means **ten times** the hydrogen ion concentration.
- **Weak** is about ionisation; **dilute** is about amount. They are independent.
- No balanced equations are required for these reactions.

questions.prompt: Hydrochloric acid and ethanoic acid are prepared at the same concentration. The hydrochloric acid has pH 1 and the ethanoic acid pH 3. Explain this difference in terms of ionisation, and state how many times greater the hydrogen ion concentration is in the hydrochloric acid.
questions.solution: Both solutions contain the same amount of acid in a given volume, because they are at the same concentration. Hydrochloric acid is a strong acid, which means it is completely ionised in aqueous solution, so almost every molecule releases a hydrogen ion. Ethanoic acid is a carboxylic acid and therefore a weak acid, which means it is only partially ionised, so at any moment most of its molecules have not released a hydrogen ion. As a result the ethanoic acid solution has a much lower concentration of hydrogen ions, and since a lower hydrogen ion concentration means a higher pH, its pH is three rather than one. The difference of two pH units means the hydrogen ion concentration in the hydrochloric acid is ten times ten, that is one hundred times, greater than in the ethanoic acid.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Start from what is the same.** Both solutions have the **same concentration**: the same amount of acid in a given volume. So the difference cannot be about how much acid is present.

**Hydrochloric acid is strong** — **completely ionised** in solution, so essentially every molecule releases its H⁺.

**Ethanoic acid is weak** — only **partially ionised**, so at any moment most molecules have **not** released their H⁺.

**The consequence.** The ethanoic acid solution has a much **lower hydrogen ion concentration**, and a lower hydrogen ion concentration means a **higher pH**: 3 rather than 1.

**The factor.** Each pH unit is a factor of 10, and the difference is 2 units:

$$10 \times 10 = 100$$

So the hydrochloric acid has **100 times** the hydrogen ion concentration.

Note what the answer avoids: it never says the ethanoic acid is *more dilute*, because it is not — that is the trap the question is set to catch.

questions.prompt: Ethanol can be converted into ethanoic acid, and ethanoic acid can be converted into an ester. Describe both conversions, naming the reagents or conditions needed, the products formed, and the functional group present at each stage.
questions.solution: Ethanol is an alcohol and contains the functional group O H. When it is treated with an oxidising agent it is oxidised to ethanoic acid, which contains the functional group C O O H. The carbon chain does not change length, so both molecules contain two carbon atoms. Ethanoic acid can then be reacted with an alcohol in the presence of an acid catalyst, usually concentrated sulfuric acid, to form an ester. If the alcohol used is ethanol, the ester formed is ethyl ethanoate, and water is also produced. The name of the ester comes in two halves, with the alcohol giving the first part, ethyl, and the acid giving the second part, ethanoate. Esters have strong sweet smells and are used in perfumes and food flavourings.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Ethanol to ethanoic acid.**

- Ethanol is an **alcohol**: functional group **–OH**.
- Treated with an **oxidising agent**, it is **oxidised** to **ethanoic acid**.
- Ethanoic acid is a **carboxylic acid**: functional group **–COOH**.
- The chain does not get longer: two carbons before, two after.

**Ethanoic acid to an ester.**

- React it with an **alcohol**, using an **acid catalyst** (usually concentrated sulfuric acid).
- With **ethanol**, the product is **ethyl ethanoate**, and **water** is formed alongside it.

**Where the name comes from.** The **alcohol** gives the first half (ethanol → **ethyl**) and the **acid** the second (ethanoic acid → **ethanoate**).

Esters have strong, sweet smells, which is why they are used in perfumes and flavourings.

The chain of functional groups is worth seeing whole: **–OH → –COOH → ester**, each step changing what the molecule does.

examTechnique.body:
Recognise a carboxylic acid by the COOH at the end of the formula, and count the carbon inside it when naming the compound.

Describe the three reactions rather than writing equations: fizzing with carbonates giving carbon dioxide, an acidic solution in water, and an ester with an alcohol using an acid catalyst.

Name an ester in two halves, the alcohol first and the acid second, and remember that water is formed alongside it.

For the Higher tier questions, the words to use are completely ionised and partially ionised. Say that the same concentration gives fewer hydrogen ions, and therefore a higher pH.

Never explain weakness by saying the acid is dilute. If the question says same concentration, it has already ruled that out.

For a pH comparison, count the units and multiply by ten for each one.
examinerErrors: Saying a weak acid is weak because it is dilute.
Forgetting to count the carbon in the COOH when naming the acid.
Naming an ester with the acid first and the alcohol second.
Saying an ester is formed without mentioning water or the acid catalyst.
Giving the pH factor as the number of units rather than ten to that power.
Saying a weak acid does not react with carbonates, when it does, only more slowly.
Writing balanced equations that are not required and are usually wrong.
Calling the -COOH group a hydroxyl group, which is the -OH of an alcohol.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer separates the substance from the solution: it explains weakness by **partial ionisation** and never reaches for the word dilute. Asked to compare two acids at the same concentration, it begins by saying what is the same before explaining what differs, which is what makes the argument land. It counts the carbon in the COOH without prompting, so CH₃COOH is ethanoic acid every time. It builds an ester's name from its two halves rather than recalling it, and remembers the water. And it knows each pH unit is a factor of ten, so a three-unit gap is a thousand, not three.
